utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Naumovski. I think we've got to paragraph 30 or 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honours, somewhere around paragraph 30. But I would just like to cover another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Naumovski: [Cont'd]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Civcija, the last question we had yesterday had to do with the organisation of the civilian police at all levels in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and my question is regarding the defence offices. Any municipality in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina they were called Secretariats for Defence. There were defence offices in each one of these municipalities. Can you tell me, they were formed in every municipality, were they civilian or military bodies?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The defence offices were definitely civilian bodies. At the level of each municipality, there was a defence office which was linked to the defence department headquartered in Mostar, and the officials in the municipal offices reported to the chief of the department in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "the head of the local office", that was -- in order for the Trial Chamber to better understand, the department was really at the level of a ministry; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I explained the structure and the organisation of the police force, it was the same with the defence. In Herceg-Bosna, there were departments for defence, for police, for other areas, and the heads had a rank of ministers, and they were all members of the government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As with the organisation of the civilian police in Central Bosnia, in addition to the defence offices at the municipal level, there was a regional office in Travnik, and then I believe it moved to Vitez. This would be parallel to the police administration. That would be the same level; that administrative body would be about the same, but it would just cover a different area?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Your Honours, I believe that Mr. Civcija covered the rise of crime in paragraph 30, so I don't think we need to revisit that topic. We can move right along and go to the events of October 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, there's one matter which I should have noted to start with. For the purposes of the transcript, Judge Robinson has returned. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had mentioned Refik Lendo, who was commander of the Territorial Defence in Novi Travnik in the latter part of 1992. Who did he replace in this position?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He replaced Mr. Saban Mandzuka, who for a while held the post of the chief of the Municipal Staff of the TO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You offered an opinion about Refik Lendo. With his arrival, were the lines of communication improved between the two sides or was it the opposite?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a big difference. While Mr. Mandzuka was commander of the TO forces, we had certain contacts and we had efforts to form a joint command in order to have both forces involved in the front line at Novi Travnik. And with certain difficulties, it worked out. But with Mr. Lendo's arrival, this changed drastically. He simply refused any kind of cooperation; Mr. Lendo, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me, in your own words but very briefly, what happened in October? Who attacked whom and why? Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly, I was not in town when the conflict broke out on that first day of the conflict. Late that day, I was on my way back and I could not enter the town because it was blocked on all sides. So I took a bypass road. I went through Fojnica, Kiseljak, Busovaca, Vitez municipalities, and only arrived in Novi Travnik from the northern side which was not under attack. According to the information I received, this was a conflict which was near -- at the gas station which was next to the HVO Novi Travnik headquarters. I believe that two members were killed in this conflict. The conflict lasted several days. A later analysis showed that the main goal of the TO forces was to take control of the Bratstvo factory, in which they succeeded, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, the real cause for this conflict was the takeover of the Bratstvo factory?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We mentioned that yesterday. The Bratstvo factory was an arms factory. They produced guns of large calibre, 230-millimetre, all up to 230-millimetre, and it was of great strategic importance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Civcija, after October 1992, did the HVO have any possibility to use the Bratstvo factory or was it out of your control for the rest of the war?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO had no access to the Bratstvo factory, and, in fact, it continues to date. Even though the war is over, the members of one ethnic group still fully control this factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one detail, perhaps. You said that the gas station was right next to the HVO military headquarters. At that time, these headquarters were in the building of the old hotel, as you called it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The military headquarters was in the building of the old hotel, and I believe I showed that yesterday on the slide which was projected. The gas station was right next to that building, and the Muslim forces wanted to take control of this gas station. Of course, the military headquarters and the HVO resisted this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1993, the section of Novi Travnik populated predominantly by Croats, did it suffer from shortages of power, water, other supplies?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, we had a very difficult year in Novi Travnik, especially the Croats who lived in the lower part of the town. When I say "the lower part of town", I mean that is the -- it was the lower ground on which we had -- Croats lived. And for the most part in 1993, Croats did not have power, and the water supply was controlled fully by Muslims and the water for the most part on 1993 was cut off. There were also some other ugly episodes. The sewer system was diverted and it was -- ran into the water supplies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In June, the fighting again flared up. Can you tell us when the conflict resumed? Who was the attacker?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In early 1993, the military forces, the ratio of the military forces changed significantly. Muslim forces received large reinforcements of troops which had been trained in the Republic of Croatia. It was the 1st and the 7th Brigades. Their primary objective was to have been fighting against the Bosnian Serbs; however, these forces together with the local Muslim forces were used in the offensive against the Croats. On the 9th June, early in the morning, this is 1993, a large offensive was launched against the municipalities of Travnik and Novi Travnik from two directions. One from the south-west and also the -- a large offensive was launched from Novi Travnik. We never expected to be attacked from that direction. This caused -- this produced a large wave of refugees, women and children who, across Mount Vilenica flooded over some -- something between 6.000 and 8.000 refugees followed by the Muslim forces. I received an order to send the entire civilian police force to Vilenica to protect further attacks from the north and this is what I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps just one comment. In spite of this large offensive which you said started on the 9th of June 1993 and despite the fact that the HVO lost certain territory, did the Novi Travnik HVO still manage to establish certain lines of defence which then remained the line of separation of two forces until the end of the conflict between the two sides?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We carried out a regrouping, as the military term goes, and we decided to defend a smaller area in order to improve its defence. Novi Travnik was literally surrounded from all sides. The units which arrived from Travnik basically reached city limits near Budosic [phoen]. The offensive launched by the Muslim forces in the south-west was fully successful and they took control of that territory so we had no more territory in the south-west. At that time, the Muslim forces controlled about 90 per cent of the territory of the municipality. It is true that the Novi Travnik municipality had a territory of 220-square kilometres and 90 per cent of that territory was controlled by the Muslim forces in June 1993, and this remained the case until the end of the conflict, that is until the signing of the Washington Accords.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Civcija, you worked for the civilian police and then for a while, you were a platoon commander at the front line. During that time when you were either in the civilian police or in the military, did you receive any orders to persecute any other -- members of any other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, certainly not. The orders which I received as a member of the police force were coming directly from the military headquarters or from the chief of the military administration [as interpreted] which, for a while, was headquartered in Travnik. I never received any orders which was directed at -- which had an aim of persecuting any ethnic group. In fact, to the contrary. I, myself, issued orders and tried to influence the situation in such a way to avoid these persecutions. I remember receiving an order once which, in its transmission to me, had passed several levels. I was a low-level commander but I know that it was signed by Colonel Blaskic which specifically forbade any type of activity which would look like persecution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just the one correction in the transcript. Page 8, line 18, you -- when you said that -- about your duties in the civilian police, that you received orders from the chief of the police administration which, for a while, was headquartered in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You -- they said military -- the transcript said "military administration" and it was "police administration"?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police administration was not a part of the military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Let's move on. As a person who was in various structures during and after -- before the war, did you ever hear that anybody, any HDZ -- that have you ever heard that there was a policy of persecution in any of these organisations?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the last topic I have regards Mr. Dario Kordic. When did you come to know Mr. Kordic and according to you, who was he? What was he? Was he a politician or a soldier?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the first democratic elections in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you know that the power was shared between the three largest parties, the Party of Democratic Action, the Serbian Democratic Party and of course the Croatian Democratic Union which, for the most part, was the party of the Croatian people. As far as I know, Mr. Kordic was a member of the main board of this party, one of its vice-presidents. I personally did not know him, nor had I heard of him until -- when we had a problem of deliveries of weapons from the Bratstvo factory when he, as a courageous and decisive man came forth and personally became involved in protests of deliveries of such weapons, and it's at that time that he gained popularity among the majority of Croatian people. Also Mr. Kordic was directly involved in negotiations with top representatives of the republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I'm referring here to the members of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Madam Biljana Plavsic, for instance, Mr. Pusina who was a deputy minister of the interior and other people, other officials who would come to Travnik when we were dealing with the weapons deliveries. Also the members of the military like General Kukanjac and others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Civcija, you're talking about 1991 and early 1992, when JNA was still deployed throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. This is what I also mentioned yesterday. This was during the terrible aggression against the Republic of Croatia, and we watched every day how the weapons which we were delivering were being used to shoot and kill civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Kordic a military commander during the war? Let's say 1993, 1994.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic, as I said, was a member of the Croatian Democratic Union, its top leadership, and he was certainly a politician. He was a politician during peacetime and he was a politician in the wartime, even though he was wearing a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Civcija, as chief of civilian police in Novi Travnik, in which position you spent some time, did you ever receive any order or directive to carry out any of your duties?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I believe that I had already answered that question; that is, from whom I received my orders. It was exclusively from the civilian police, the military headquarters, and at one point from General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were in the military, did you ever receive -- did you ever hear that Mr. Kordic issued orders through the chain of command of Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I became a soldier, I received my orders exclusively from my superiors in the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade. That was from the commander of the 3rd Battalion and from the commander of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade. I never heard that Mr. Kordic issued any orders to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Civcija. This concludes my examination-in-chief, Your Honours. Cross-examined by Mr. Mikulicic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Civcija, I represent Mr. Cerkez' Defence, and I will be very brief with you. I have only several questions. This Trial Chamber has already heard and it is also obvious from your testimony that there were three conflicts between the Muslim and Croatian forces in Novi Travnik in June '92, in October '92, and the large offensive in June 1993. You told us yesterday that after the first conflict, there was an informal division of town, so that the Croatian population sort of concentrated in one area of town and the Muslim in the other, and this is the situation that is still there today; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you, sir, is: Do you remember that after the second conflict in October '92 and the third conflict in June 1993 in the territory of Novi Travnik, there were any significant military conflicts between the two sides?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no significant military conflicts, even though there were a number of incidents in town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, de facto, a status quo which was reached after the second conflict was maintained?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave evidence yesterday that with the aggression against the Republic of Croatia, a significant number of BiH citizens went to provide assistance to Croatia to defend itself against the JNA and the Serbian paramilitary troops, and I believe that you mentioned something like 15.000 people.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said about 15.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [French interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have to interrupt. We're getting French on our channel.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Is this better now? I think we're all right, we're back on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We seem to be back on track.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: May I continue? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall repeat the question, for the sake of the transcript. Of those 15.000 men who went to the Republic of Croatia from Bosnia to help the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia, they included also quite a number of Muslims from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were some Muslims too. But what their share was, I really wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it true that when the war broke out in Bosnia, those men who were members of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia went back to their native areas and placed themselves at the disposal to participate in a defence against the aggressor in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite a number of them returned to defend their homeland.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that holds true of both Croats and Muslims, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Both Muslims and Croats returned to defend their homeland, but quite a number of their colleagues stayed back in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Civcija. We have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just to inform the Chamber, Mr. Nice will not be present during this cross-examination, if the Chamber has no objection. Thank you very much. Cross-examined by Ms. Somers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Civcija, I would like to get a little more information from you, if I could, please, about your background. You are a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you have indicated. Are you also a citizen of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which passport did you use to come to The Hague, if I may ask?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used the only passport that I have, and that is the passport of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not have, as I understand it, a passport from Bosnia-Herzegovina at all.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have a passport of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because if you have the passport of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you need a visa to go to a large number of countries, and that comes very costly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your move -- is it to Grahovo? Where is that, please, what municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Grahovo is a municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is it located?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is located in Canton 10 in Herceg-Bosna. It is in the south-western part of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the Muslim population of Grahovo?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very small.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you give a percentage? You've been able to give percentages generally. Would you give us a percentage, please, of the total population?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you like this: There are about five or six hundred inhabitants in Grahovo, and if you want the percentage of Muslims, they are about one per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One per cent. Thank you. When did you join the HDZ first?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was your activity at the time limited to any particular area?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, but could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your HDZ activity restricted to any particular area of Bosnia or of any other place where the HDZ was active?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1990, I lived in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is where you were an active member of the HDZ; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I became a member of the Croatian Democratic Union.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your work as a legal advisor in the Bratstvo factory, did you draft contracts, did you do actual legal work?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not draw up any contracts. But in the early days of my career, I represented my company in court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you oversee or approve contracts which were issued by the appropriate persons in Bratstvo?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean commercial deals, they were concluded by the department -- by the section for commerce, and I was not their superior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you part of the chain that would know that certain contracts were being issued, such as contracts for the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked for the Bratstvo factory, but I must explain what is the Bratstvo factory. It is a system of several plants, and I began my career in one of those plants which was engaged, however, in the manufacture of tractors rather than weapons. I did not work in the plant which was manufacturing weapons, so that I could not approve any contracts regarding deliveries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was something you called a joint administration unit. Did that cover all of the various units of Bratstvo? You indicated that there were different items produced. You were in the joint area, overseeing all?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The last four years in Bratstvo, I was the head of the joint administration unit of the whole factory, that is, of the whole compound system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during your time there, were there always contracts for the production and sale of weapons for the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are asking me a question which refers to the top-most leadership of this system, and that was the management, the steering board, that was the collective body. So your question will be answered by a question of its member, and I was simply the head of technical service which was serving the needs of that management body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then your answer to my question is that you do not know if there were at all times contracts with the JNA during your time there. Is that the answer?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar. I'm not aware of that activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you became a lawyer, that was during the years of the Federal Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please help us, I'm not familiar with the process of becoming a lawyer. Is there any type of oath to uphold, any type of constitution, or what is the nature of the ceremony of induction into lawyering; can you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One completes the secondary school, enrolls in the faculty of law, graduates from it, and then you get your -- you obtain the diploma which says that you are a lawyer, a jurist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to appear in the courts, which you indicated you did, do you have to pass any type of, as we call it, a bar exam or is there some type of oath of allegiance to the government or sovereign which empowers you to act as a lawyer. That is my question.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. To appear in court to represent somebody or to become a judge, you have to take a special examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever appear in a constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with its function?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you appeared on behalf of Bratstvo, did you appear in the courts of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I appeared in courts of Yugoslavia, not in courts of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: ... of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, there were five more republics in addition to Bosnia-Herzegovina and two autonomous provinces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were your appearances?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before courts in business disputes in Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, Croatia, Vojvodina, Kosovo. The only place I did not appear before the court was in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, a document was produced by your Defence counsel, apparently supplied by you, that showed an approval or -- an approval to the position for Ministry of Internal Affairs. Who actually nominated you? The approval is by Mate Boban but this court has seen a series of documents for various police chief positions that indicate there is an approval, but a nomination process. Who nominated you for that position?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know exactly, but I suppose it was done by the president of the municipal board, rather the president of the HVO in the municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you're not sure who nominated you actually and carried your name forward.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the president of the Croat Defence Council in the municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you give the name, please?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the municipal or rather the Croat Defence Council of Novi Travnik at that time was Mr. Jozo Sekic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also produced from 1992 a document which is dated July 3rd, but you indicated that it actually took effect the 13th of June, which was an appointment or an approval for an appointment to head, let's see now, head of the Department of Internal Affairs in Novi Travnik. Now, that, again, was signed by Mate Boban, but who advanced or nominated you for the position in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the Croat Defence Council, Mr. Jozo Sekic, and I'm positive about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did he do that? When was it done? When was he actually advancing your name?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in May, late May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you can help -- there seems to be some conflict in what this Court has heard before then. There has been testimony by witnesses that your name was among six names presented for positions for Croats only on the 28th of May, 1992 by Dario Kordic. Can you help clarify this confusion, please?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic may have said his view or given his consent or something, approval or something like that, but the nomination came from the president of the HVO in Novi Travnik. And as for my appointment as the chief of the interior, that appointment was not signed by Mr. Boban but by the minister, Brana Kvesic. At that time he was the chief of the Department of the Interior of the Croat Community. That is something like a minister in government, and he was the one who took that decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the decision which you presented yesterday, D219/1 is signed by Mate Boban as president and it is labelled, "Decision on Appointed Department Heads and Members of the Municipal HVO of Novi Travnik." There does appear to be, in the distribution, an archive. Could you tell us where we might check anything more where this archive would be located, please.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I should like to ask to be able to fairly answer these questions to know when the Prosecution asks me about a document, then I think I need to see that document with my eyes. Because now one document is mentioned, now another document is mentioned. So could I please have them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If it's necessary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is it necessary to get into this?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Well, I'd simply like to know if we can be instructed as to where such an archive exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Show the witness the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Then I'll move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you're looking at your document please in the lower left-hand corner, the one that is marked -- it's stated Mostar, 3 July, 1992, it's the distribution list. Point number four is an archive, and I just wondered if you could tell us where that archive would be.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know the answer to your question. The document that I brought with me is in the -- is in my wife's archive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your wife's archive? I'm sorry, did I understand that correctly? The archive -- are you suggesting that Mate Boban distributed the document to your wife's archive? I'm asking you about the archive mentioned on this document. Where would that archive as a body of HZ HB or HVO be?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I fully understand you, and I answered your question the last time that I do not know where that archive is. And as regards this document, it was served on me personally, and I left it with my wife and she kept it all this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had been asked about customs and respecting customs of the different ethnic groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina. When did you perceive a change, and this would have been relevant to your point number six that you testified to, when did you actually feel a change in the relations and how did it come about?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A significant change occurred at the time of fierce attacks on the Republic of Croatia and at a time when Croats not only in the Novi Travnik municipality but across Central Bosnia, I should say, remonstrated and requested that something be done and not to take the weapons out of the Bratstvo factory for the army which was attacking their countrymen in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this change exacerbated, as you perceived it, by the imposition of the Croat Community of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna upon a non-Croat population. How did you see that as a person in the public sector?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, I said that it was a very difficult period of time. A state had fallen apart. Others were emerging. At some point, we were left without the federal state and had not yet acquired our own state, and people feared the unknown or what lay ahead. And we knew of the grave threat of the then biggest power, and that was the power of Serbia which at that time controlled the JNA. We knew that it did not want Yugoslavia to be dissolved, and that any area where Serb people lived had to be part of that Yugoslavia and the same held true of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At that time, there were different approaches to the solution, to the situation and we sensed that there would be an aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina as well, and wanted to get ready for the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you are referring to when the aggression started against Croatia. What date do you pin that to?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on several occasions. It began on Plitvice, Pakrac, Bele Vode, [indiscernible] attack on Vukovar, on Dubrovnik, Osijek, Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Date, please.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was summer of '91. That is, autumn of '91.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were suggesting in your testimony that -- I think you used the term "unconcerned", that the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was not concerned, or the leadership was. That is a very strong statement, as was pointed out by Mr. Mikulicic. Certain persons from Bosnia-Herzegovina, including Muslims, went to assist in the fighting of Croatia, but what about the assistance to the defence of Dubrovnik that was lent? Your comment on that, the ability to have Croatian troops positioned by agreement to defend from Bosnia the attack on Dubrovnik? Is that a lack of concern?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecutor completely misinterprets in this question the answer that I gave yesterday. I was not -- or I didn't precisely say the leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina was unconcerned. I said political representatives of the people called the Muslims were unconcerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd have to ask you to give examples of failure to show concern, if you can do that, please.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be logical for the highest -- for the top officials of my country, Bosnia-Herzegovina, to issue orders and prohibit the export of weapons for JNA at the time of fighting, at the time when this army was attacking the Republic of Croatia, and such orders never came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that all commerce will stop as a result of this; is this the suggestion? I mean correct us if we're wrong, but we've seen a fair amount of evidence that there was trade, albeit perhaps black-marketing, but trade between and among all parties during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, there was trade, and I did not think at that time and I do not think now that trade should be prohibited or any kind of local economy. But there is a sea of difference between flour and meat, on one hand, and guns which kill your children, on the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there a difference between gasoline, that fuels the equipment to carry and transport that, and the guns?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we've heard enough now about this topic. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, about your -- excuse me, let me just make sure. You mentioned that there were times when the Croats stopped and turned back shipments of weapons that were being exported for the use of the JNA. Did you, in fact, participate in those events? Were you personally involved?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was involved, but as the chief of the Public Security Station. That was the duty that I held at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had discussed also a point that I would just like to ask you perhaps to flush out a little bit. You talked about widespread discrimination against Muslims and Croats under the former Yugoslav existence. Discrimination by whom?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word "discrimination" can also mean that a people enjoys more rights than other peoples. When it comes to the former Yugoslavia, in my testimony yesterday I said clearly that all or almost all executive posts in the police, the army, public sector, public companies, were mostly held by members of one people. In the army, it was so drastic that about 90 per cent of all the officers came from one people only. In the police --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just ask you, the term you use, though, in connection with this, the Serbs I'm going to assume is the group you're talking about. Is that correct, the Serbs? That's what you indicated. You said "privileged". You didn't talk about and insist on any rights. You simply said "privileged". Where is the discrimination? If you can't in a couple of words sum it up, then don't, but is that what you are referring to, privilege as opposed to deprivation of rights?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a man is privileged, then to me it means that another one is deprived of his right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think I'll have to move on from there. It's beyond my ability to challenge at this point. Were you in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you serve?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I served in the town of Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had discussed the referendum, and I wanted to see how much you participated in the events leading up to the referendum for independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Did you participate as early as, let's say, 1991 in meetings in Busovaca where Dario Kordic was beginning to gain some prominence in the HDZ party?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you be more specific, please? What period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, this would be, I would say, July, August '91.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, there was a connection, was there not? The HDZs pretty much followed the developments in each other's municipalities, is that a fair statement, to know what was going on?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one could say that there was a link between the HDZ in various municipalities, which is normal in all parties throughout the world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you follow any of the dialogue or perhaps polemics between Dario Kordic and another HDZ member by named Dragutin Zvonimir Cicak; were you aware of some of the interchanges and exchanges between them?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you read the local papers, which carried some of the articles that were written and exchanged by those two persons?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not read them, and it is the first time that I actually hear about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you following closely the developments of the HDZ Travnik Regional Community meeting on the 12th of November, '91 -- did that attract your attention -- just prior to the decision creating Herceg-Bosna? Were you following it carefully?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend that meeting, so that I couldn't really follow what went on there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of a meeting, though?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I hear about it for the first time from you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your position on the establishment of Herceg-Bosna? Did you favour it? Did you take it to your constituency, the people with whom you were in the HDZ and the other municipal representatives of the other parties?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: By following the events in Croatia and before that in Slovenia, I was aware that something similar would also happen in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And if you're interested in my personal views, my desire was to do something to become organised so that this would be prevented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that what would be prevented, the potential violence, the potential for war; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. The war was threatening Bosnia-Herzegovina because, first of all, our political representatives in the top -- in the highest political bodies could not agree on a common state or how it is supposed to look. Two ethnic groups wanted that state but could not agree on the arrangements for it, and one ethnic group, the Serbs, for the most part did not want this state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the HDZ in '91, headed by Kljuic, seemed to be on the same track with regard to the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina as with the position of the Muslims. Where was the division?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be so kind as to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, of course. You were talking about two ethnic groups who wanted the state but could not agree on the arrangements for it, and you've excluded the Serbs as being in that. So that would only leave the Muslims and the Croats. Now, just looking back from all the evidence which has been before this Court, the HDZ, as represented by Stjepan Kljuic as the president of it, was clearly, as you use the term, on the same wavelength as the remaining group of Muslims wanting an integral Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, you referred to a division or a disagreement. Where was the disagreement? Could you pinpoint it, please, and with whom did it lie?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basis of this agreement was that the Croatian political representatives wanted to build in some kind of protective mechanism so that the Croats, as one of the three equal constituent groups, would not disappear, so that if you had the democratic principles of one person, one vote, and not build in these protective mechanisms for a minority population which only had a share of 17.4 per cent in the total population, this group would then, under those principles, disappear. The political representatives wanted to build in a mechanism so that certain strategic decisions would not be adopted without a consensus of all people, and I fully understand that. And after all, this was built into the Dayton Accords too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which political representatives in 1991 wanted this? I don't recall Mr. Kljuic advocating this position.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic was not the only representative of the Croatian people, even though he was very highly placed. I remember following debates in the BiH parliament, and when I say "politicians" -- when I mention politicians, there were a number of Croatian politicians who took part in these parliamentary debates and pointed out this problem. I repeat, these protective mechanisms of the constituent role or attributes of a people were built into the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this fixation, for lack of a better word, on being 17 per cent affect you when it was still the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia? Did you feel the same concern for the percentage of Croats within the territory?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The former State of Yugoslavia was a socialist country. In socialism, a completely different set of rules were in force. There was one leader, there was one party. Even though Yugoslavia was one of the most liberal socialist countries, we could not be happy with the level of democracy and human rights in that country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was really specific, it was about a 17 per cent minority. Did that concern you at that period of time? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I get your view on a comment by Ignac Kostroman which was passed in January of 1992 in the Busovaca Cultural Club. It was attended by Dario Kordic and celebrating the recognition of the Republic of Croatia. Mr. Kostroman was quoted as saying, and this has been presented before to the Court, that "This ..." Busovaca, "... was Croatian land. Croatian laws will be enforced here and those who would not obey the Croatian laws would have to leave." Do you share those sentiments with respect to your role in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not at that meeting. I didn't quite understand when it was held, so I cannot offer any comments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 16 January, 1992, after the recognition of Croatia. Now, I realise that you don't recognise that you were not there. I'm asking you just about the sentiment which is in a neighbouring community which was a seminal part of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Do you share that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is very difficult for me to comment on the views which have been extracted out of contexts. I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the difficulty? All you're being asked is to say whether you agree or not agree with the views. Can you answer the question or would you rather not?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer any question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, do you agree with that sentiment or not?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can it please be repeated for me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure, I would be happy to read it back to you. It was at the Busovaca Cultural Club and it was a speech, a part of a speech given by Ignac Kostroman on the occasion of the recognition of the Republic of Croatia and what he said was this, referring to Busovaca, "... was Croatian land. Croatian laws would be enforced here and those who would not obey the Croatian laws would have to leave."

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree with that comment even though it has been taken out of a context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you actively advocating the referendum for independence? You indicated yesterday that without the Croat vote, there would not have been an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina. What did you do to advance that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply put, I went to the referendum, I even took my little daughter with me and she shook hands with the then president of the -- whose name I believe was Mr. Cengic at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have to be swayed in your enthusiasm simply because this Court has had a fair amount of evidence about the resistance by the HDZ to the referendum and very much last minute through, as it were, communication with Mate Boban, the Croat Community was urged to get out and vote. Were you sitting on the fence at any point or was this consistently your viewpoint?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was absolutely prepared for the Bosnia and Herzegovina being an independent state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made some reference, which I'd just like to address while we're chronologically, at least, numerically, rather, on it, to a massive influx of refugees into the area. And I wonder if you could provide documentation about numbers and the impact. Where did you draw the figures or the reference "massive"? What kind of numbers are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will very gladly answer your question. After the siege of Sarajevo started and the shelling, efforts were made to pull out the women, children, the elderly and the ill out of town and one of these convoys reached the town of Ilijas where it was stopped by the armed Serbian soldiers and they kept it for two or three days. We were regularly informed about this. It was covered in the media. And the pressure was exerted on the Serbian side to release those civilians; women, children, and it was a matter of time when they would do it. Meanwhile in Novi Travnik, we were preparing, that is, members of all three ethnic groups; Croats, Muslims and Serbs, we were preparing ourselves, in other words, to receive these people, to accommodate them, to provide them food, shelter, facilities to wash. And I remember that we provided organisations so that the first night after all the trouble and all the humiliation that they were subjected to, they could rest up. All these people, the next day, were sent towards the Republic of Croatia independent on the means of transportation. Then later on, some stayed in Croatia and some went to points beyond depending on which countries at that time were willing to receive some of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, maybe that's where you can help us a little bit because the -- what I read from your summary and what I got from your testimony was that these people hung around and caused a permanent problem. Now, the Court has seen on a number of occasions and you have not but there was a document, Z223 which is from the 22nd of September, 1992, which certainly would cover the periods involved. I just want to cite you some of it, it is a document that is signed by Kostroman, Valenta and Kordic. And the points that I want to extract from there on this matter is -- would it help to have it in front of you on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it's not a matter for the witness, it's a matter for the Court. We must move quickly through this. If you're going to put a document to a witness, he should have it in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think it's a very important point, so if I may ask the usher to put it up, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's the part that says, "Situation in municipalities," it would be on the second page of the English. I do not have a copy of the Croatian, I'm sorry, and it's a Novi Travnik report. It talks about generally -- it talks about refugees, but it indicates that, "It has been noted that there are criminals in the military police that are carrying on with their military activities..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm doing that deliberately, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "The town is fairly well supplied. Refugees have mostly been passing through on their way to Croatia, but recently refugees have been coming in." I don't see, and correct me if I am wrong, a real concern about shortages that were alluded to by you yesterday or any aspect of criminality by refugees. Is it possible this material was based on incorrect information?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may answer your question, I believe that you misunderstood my evidence yesterday. I spoke about refugees in two ways. A moment ago, I explained what the situation was like in Novi Travnik when the first convoy of refugees arrived, and I pointed out that these were the refugees from Sarajevo. After that, a large offensive of the Serbian army ensued in Krajina, that is the northern and northwestern Bosnia. From this area, the refugees -- there was a flood of refugees, mostly the Muslims, who started moving in the direction of Travnik municipality. In addition, at that time in Travnik, the majority of the Serbian population was fully informed about the impending offensive of the Serbian troops so a large number of Serbian inhabitants started leaving in the direction of the areas controlled by the army of Bosnian Serbs so there were a lot of abandoned homes. After they left, this new wave of refugees arrived. There were tens of thousands of them who doubled and tripled the size of the population in both Travnik and Novi Travnik, because I also went to Travnik and saw large numbers of people sleeping in parks who were arriving in columns over a number of days. We made efforts in both of these towns, both sides did, both the Muslim and the Croat sides, to organise these people. They started taking the Serbian homes, abandoned homes, and then we started looking for accommodation for them in some communal places because we ran out of space. We did everything we could to create conditions for the reception of these people to provide them with meals, to give them something to -- to cover themselves. Some of them would just come with bundles of belongings so we did what we could to provide them assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I realise that you've given an expansive answer, but the point is that as of September, 1992, there was no observation that this was causing the type of problem that was allude -- that you suggested that it was causing. And I wanted also -- in terms of the crime situation that you mentioned yesterday in connection with refugees, there's a document that you, yourself, or your office issued. I wonder if you could comment on. There are two, Z518.3 and Z565.1. Looking first at 565.1, I'm sorry, that's coming to you second. We'll have to wait a minute. Let me ask you while we're distributing it, can you help us and tell us as a police officer or as a police executive, did you have a mechanism in place for capturing crime statistics?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And very briefly, can you just tell us what that was? How did you capture your statistics?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every crime that was committed would be registered in log books which we had with the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then if there was a mechanism in place for registering them, if you take a look please at 565.1, it bears the stamp of your office. It is unclear whether it is exactly your signature or someone perhaps subordinate, but it seems to say "Zapojednik", and this is a summary submitted but your office, possibly by you for crimes, it's a crime report for 1992. And just looking at it, it -- just highlighting it actually, there were -- let's see it would be the second page, a couple of cases of suicide for employees of the police station. There was some traffic accidents. You said the courts were not working. You've not issued any requests for criminal charges, but perhaps the courts -- maybe you could explain that. And then optimistically, you indicated that a large number of criminal acts or a large amount of criminal cases were solved with the perpetrators being arrested, statements taken from them in order to bring criminal charges, and that most of the goods stolen from apartments and vehicles were returned to their own owners. You've mentioned 129 criminal acts, mainly banditry, burglary, vehicle and other theft. Is that terribly different from any other type of community crime report? 21

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me object to the form of that question. There are really two sets of questions, a whole set of propositions, using the word "you".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness comment on it. He's got the document in front of him.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go ahead, please. Please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I was asking was to comment on essentially whether or not this is an unusual amount of crime. You do have some training, I assume, in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. Is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just don't interrupt. Ms. Somers, will you wait until I finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just wait. You've seen that document. Does it set out a fair picture of the crime that was committed in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but only in the section of town controlled by this police station because, Your Honours, in late 1992, early 1993, the town was divided into two, and both police forces, the Croatian and the Muslim ones, had the zone of responsibility which was under its control.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I enquire further, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, so these documents -- this document does not capture, then, what was happening to a whole other segment of the population within your municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that this document refers to the area controlled by the Novi Travnik police station, which is the territory controlled by the armed forces of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Croat factors or figures only here. If you look, please, at the other document, 518.3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If we're moving on to the other document, that might be a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sure. It's a very brief one, Judge. Would you want me to get rid of it first and then move on to another subject area altogether?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I think we'll have our break. And, Ms. Somers, if you could bring matters to a close as rapidly as you can, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'll try. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Judge May, if I may just take a moment, I wanted -- in reviewing the transcript, I wanted to express my apology. I was not following carefully the fact that you were asking a question of the witness, and therefore the interruptions. I will proceed. I just wanted to make sure that it was -- it was not intentional.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Document 518.3 bears only a few minutes' worth of review. If you would take a look at it, please. It's from March 1993, and it simply again is a capture, very quickly, of the February statistics. If you would just confirm that this is accurate: that you reported only 25 burglaries, two armed robberies, three attempted murders, two murders with known perpetrators, and you list some of the dispositions, and disturbing the peace would be another type of crime. Is this accurate? Does this reflect the crime statistics for that month?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a question about a point you mentioned on the other side of town. You indicated there were a separate set of institutions -- "parallel," I believe, is the term you used -- and the separate Muslim police department. If the crime situation within the municipality became so severe, would you assist the Muslim side in trying to control it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a time, there was some kind of cooperation. I think that the policemen manifested solidarity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did that stop?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since there were two different systems of the work of police stations as of June, '92, it stopped when the conflicts escalated, and they escalated, once again, in the spring of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having raised the issue of two different systems, it appears that you were the only person, at least in my scanning the evidence, to have asserted that the Muslims set up a parallel system. On what do you base that? What documentation shows the Muslims setting it up?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say anything about documents, but I can speak about the time and events. There was a parallel police station, there was a parallel army. That was the Territorial Defence, consisting of members of the Muslim people. And there was the civilian authority, the so-called War Presidency of Novi Travnik, including only representatives of the Muslim people. On the side which was controlled by the Croat Defence Council, I have already explained the situation there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You yourself indicated that after the multi-party elections, there was a form of cooperation. Can you please comment on the version that has been presented to this Court, which suggests that it, in fact, was the Croat ethnic group that set up its own separate institutions to the exclusion of the Muslims? How do you view that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, I was shown and testified about the document -- and you showed it today also -- relating to the establishment of the authority of the Croat Defence Council in the municipality of Novi Travnik, and the institutions of that authority, that is, the government, included three members of Muslim ethnicity, which means that members of both peoples participated in the government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened? Is it possible that the witnesses and the multiple documents attesting to the Croat initiative in creating separateness are wrong?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot speak about something that I have neither seen nor heard, but, as I have said, there is a document and there are people who throughout the war were members of the Croat Defence council, and also members of the HVO government, Muslims who were in the Safet Koco, Mr. Feriz Rizvic, who was a construction engineer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the third member, the interpreter, I'm sorry, missed the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were the Muslim police thrown out of the police station that had once been a joint police station?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you followed my testimony yesterday carefully, I said that in June 1992, what was the target and purpose of the attack on the Territorial Defence made of Muslim members, it was all the strategic places around the town. Nobody ever expelled Muslim policemen from the police. They kept coming to work for several days, and then one day they simply stopped coming because they had been ordered to do so by somebody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On June 19th there was a meeting in the workers' hall, I believe my date is correct. Following that meeting, you and two other, at least two other soldiers, took out Ragib Zukic and Salih Krnjic and proceeded to beat Mr. Zukic into unconsciousness and to incarcerate in the Cafe Grand Mr. Krnjic. Can you please explain what motivated that on a police executive?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The first question is did this, in fact, happen?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I testified about it yesterday. I said that I found Mr. Salih Krnjic with a couple of soldiers treating him inhumanly, trying to beat him or rather beating him and I protected him. And this other gentleman, I did not see nor heard, nor hear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you heard about what happened to them ultimately, and did you hear about these assaults later, were they reported to you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it loudly and clearly that I protected Mr. Krnjic, and I took him in my vehicle to the lower part of the town and provided him with safe accommodation. In the morning I turned him over to Colonel Filip Filipovic, the local HVO commander, and he took him to the village of Kasapovici where the Territorial Defence was headquartered and left him there. And Mr. Jozo Sekic, President of the Croat Defence Council of Novi Travnik came back with me on that day. He was detained the next day near the intersection of the fire brigade by members of the Territorial Defence manned by Muslim soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Krnjic beaten at the time you took him into custody for his own safety?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had I not protected him, before I protected him, he received several blows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Cafe Grand is owned by whom?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The owner of the cafe is Mr. Marinko Marelja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was also a high-ranking member of the HVO in your municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of his having raised money to finance the publication of Anto Valenta's book?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He participated in the funding to help publish that book and some other people too, those who were better off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the book I mean the book on the separation of populations, the voluntary resettlement of population. Are you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with that book. That book was often the subject of discussion at various meetings held abroad among representatives of all three peoples with the mediation of the international community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What types of discussions surrounded the book?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, when there are conflicts going on, and in our country the international community sent its representatives to our country they were Lord Owen, Mr. Stoltenberg, Mr. Vance. And there was several discussions of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the manner of its organisation. And I suppose that that book and many other materials must have been used in different plans which are known under different names, as you must be aware of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not, but I perused it, and I saw that it contains a lot of statistical data and maps. The appearance of Bosnia-Herzegovina before that and all the models of how to arrange it, how to organise it and the like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The theme of the book was discussed at the meetings with the International Community, was it not? The theme of separation of populations? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were several documents which were to serve as a basis for the organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and this book, in all likelihood, was also used for such plans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to comment on your views having just perused it or is that not possible to do?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't really say anything interesting about that book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the -- excuse me. Again, you were the first person to put before us as far as I could go through the evidence and understand that the October 1992 conflict was initiated by the Muslims. Do you have documents that can back that up?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it loudly and clearly that the first day of conflict -- excuse me, what month did you mention?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it clearly that on the first day of the conflict, I was not in the town, and the conflict allegedly started with the attack on the gas station which was next to the military staff, and that was the -- however the information that I received after I returned to Novi Travnik, and I already described how I came to the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Though you claim you were not in town, can you tell me: Were you aware of checkpoints being set up in advance of this incident?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, could you repeat that question? I don't quite understand it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although you were not in -- you claim not to have been in Novi Travnik on that date, are you aware of checkpoints having been erected prior to this incident? I can ask you specifically if you'd like. Are you aware of a checkpoint that was visited by Dario Kordic in Novi Travnik on the 17th of October?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know which checkpoint was visited by Mr. Dario Kordic. And as for the setting up of checkpoints, yes, of course I know about them, because they began to be set up a long time before that and they were changed from time to time. We set up those checkpoints even before the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who set them up? You said "we". To whom are you referring?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, initially the checkpoints were manned by police members, including the reserve force, under the orders we received from the Ministry of the Interior or, rather, it was the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which took the decision insisting on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated that no order had ever been given to you, as far as you knew, by Dario Kordic. Again, turning to an exhibit which is already in evidence, and just for reference it is October 21st, 1992, which is Z243 -- before I ask you specifically to address this, may I just ask you, where were you on the 21st of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were not in the midst of the things happening that you claim were tantamount to an attack by the ABiH. What were you doing?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the day when I arrived in Novi Travnik or the 21st?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 21st.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 21st, the fighting was under way in the town, and I was with members of the police in the premises in the lower part of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But when you cite specifically the fighting beginning, what day; 20th, 21st, 19th? Give a specific date, please.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was the 19th that the fighting began.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever meet with Colonel Bob Stewart from BritBat in Novi Travnik or anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew Colonel Bob Stewart, and I was present at a couple of meetings which he also attended. However, I do not remember that we ever met one on one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present in Novi Travnik on the 20th of October, when Colonel Bob Stewart went to see Dario Kordic and came to the conclusion that without Kordic's authority, no cease-fire agreement could happen?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall being with Mr. Bob Stewart then, and I do not know what Mr. Bob Stewart said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at the document that I did ask to have brought to you, if you look at the last item, item 10 -- and of course this document is on the situation in Novi Travnik, authored by Blaskic and Dario Kordic -- can you comment, please? "While defence operations are being conducted, the vice-president of the HZ HB, Dario Kordic, and I in Novi Travnik, continuously leading the military operations with deep knowledge of the situation and by keeping all the forces under control, Commander" -- and then there's a slight illegibility in English -- "Filipovic is also here at the Novi Travnik HVO HQ." Does this order bind you? Would anything that Kordic may have done to implement this position, would it have bound you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I met both Mr. Kordic and Mr. Blaskic. Of course, I would be bound only by orders coming from Mr. Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attempt to reach out to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the number of that document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That was, Your Honour, 243, Z243.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever attempt to try to reach any type of accord with your Muslim counterparts?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, yes. After the conflict, a meeting was organised in the new hotel in Novi Travnik, attended by representatives of both sides. I believe some had come from Mostar and some from Sarajevo. And there we agreed on the cessation of fighting, abolition of checkpoints, and some other matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there success?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was successfully done, and the fighting stopped after that meeting which, as I said, took place in the hotel in Novi Travnik. I can't remember the date exactly, but I believe it was some seven or eight days after the conflict broke out in October '92. So it could have been perhaps the 25th or the 26th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were working, according to your --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your microphone, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were working, according to your evidence, in Mostar for a ministry, and how long did you hold that position? How long into 1995 did you hold that position?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, first Foreign and then Interior. I worked for the Ministry of the Interior from May '95 to April '96.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then prior to that, you were working for the Ministry of -- I didn't catch that, please. There was another ministry you were working for? Oh, Foreign Affairs. And who was the minister?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, excuse me. You said that I worked for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. I'm not a diplomat, I never was that, and I don't think I shall ever be, so that I never worked for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. I was always only with the Ministry of the Interior, and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry. The transcript does read "Foreign", so perhaps I misconstrued something you said. So you were in Mostar in 1995, in November?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CIVCIJA [Resumed]
