Each of those documents has got to be separately tracked, some to be returned, some to go to the Registry and, frankly, the risk of loss of a document is very much greater in those circumstances than under the practices which presently obtain. Indeed under the practices which presently obtain, as I understand it, there has been no loss of a document that we're aware of so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: These are arguments you can apply in any court and what you're suggesting is that the body which is responsible for the administration of the court is incapable of keeping a document secure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I didn't say that. I said that our systems are preferable, more secure, and less likely to lead to error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you may be right saying they may be more secure, but in matters of this kind, I am sure you will be sensitive to the matters in that justice must also be done, but be seen to be done. I, personally, am concerned about the impression that this will give to the International Community that exhibits are in the hands of a party to the proceedings. I mean that is now -- how does that appear to the International Community, first of all, that exhibits on the basis of which the Tribunal must determine the guilt or innocence of an accused person is in the hands of a party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In my respectful submission, your sensitivity is well understood and appreciated, but in the particular circumstances of this and these cases, not what should be the guiding principle for this reason. The reason that nearly all documents remain undisturbed in the vaults of the evidence unit, disturbed so far as the dedicated custodians of that unit are concerned, because it's not an unit which I have access, save on specific protocols or whatever it may be, is because in nearly all cases, the documents are not required to be seen in their original form. In our case, unless I've forgotten something, I don't think any document was required to be seen in its original form up and until yesterday. I may have forgotten one, and that's hardly surprising with ECMM reports, BritBat reports and so on. If, at any stage, any document is required to be seen then, of course, its production is called for, up it comes. Interestingly enough, when this matter was first ventilated, Mr. Sayers raised the issue of a Jelisic document. Unfortunately, it was a quotation completely out of context. And since it seemed to be being launched at me, I will just take time to explain actually what happened there, for it rather supports the general proposition that I am advancing. What happened was that a witness turned up and out of his own back pocket produced something. It was a pass that he said was signed by Jelisic. It was copied and it was agreed all around that the case was going to proceed on the basis of a copy. There was then some cross-examination as to its genuineness and indeed as to the issue of whether any such pass had ever been issued. But unfortunately, given that the defendant in his interview had acknowledged drafting such a pass. An application was made by Defence counsel by that particular original document should stay in court. But the judges, at that stage, ordered otherwise and they said, "No, we will carry on dealing with the copy." The judges then, as was the practice in that court, asked their questions which were many. One of those questions, not from Judge Riad as the note suggests, but from Judge Rodrigues, returned to the issue of the genuineness of the document. It seemed to me, and perhaps I was actually being sympathetic to Defence counsel that where this issue was alive, whatever the problems he faced arising from the interview of this defendant, it might be preferable for the document to stay here in The Hague rather than to return to the witness. So what I was doing there was reflecting an exception to the general rule but rather than to incur the wrath of the bench by suggesting that their initial ruling was wrong, I suggested to them that in light of the Judge's question, the way the judges might want to investigate handwriting, and for that reason the document might remain in court and indeed so it did. But that's the history of that, and that again shows the general practice that copies were acceptable, save in exceptional and articulated circumstances. Here and in any of these cases, these documents are, of course, available for inspection by the Defence, if they ask to see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not the inspection which is in issue, it's the custody of the exhibits which is in issue. I don't think we're going to get very much further with this, except to really enquire as to what the sensitive exhibits are and, particularly, the audiotape which is, in my view, something which should clearly have been from the outset, once it was produced, in the custody of the Registry and not in the custody of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I do two things? First of all, can I distribute perhaps for reading overnight the institutional response? It's not signed, but I hope you'll accept it in its present form.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's what I meant, the OTP. "Jargon", well, yes, jargon, the OTP's institution. There it is. The audiotape --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. You can have it now. While that's being distributed, can I turn to the tape. What's true for documents is true for all forms of tapes as well. They come to the building and they are copied. At the time of that tape, there weren't digital copying facilities. I think there are now. Would the Court rather read this document first, or should I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, let's hear this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's hear me; right. Now, the history of the audiotape is not uninteresting, for matters have never been fully articulated on the Defence side. What happened was that the tape arrived -- the first tape arrived here. It was copied immediately. That, therefore, was the master copy. It was distributed to the Defence, and they were invited to deal with whether the voices were the voices of Kordic and Blaskic. They acknowledged that they were. Nothing was said as to the nature of challenge to that tape, save questions in the most imprecise format about it, and then at a later stage from Mr. Stein, a reference to the possibility of words, odd words, being added in. The witness came and gave evidence about the tape. On that occasion, I think the original, as produced by the witness, was signed out under chain of custody to come to court to be played. The witness produced from his briefcase another version, I think one in time that hadn't even left his possession. That was played for a short period of time, but the Court concluded that it was too difficult to make use of as a piece of real evidence and that it had to be listened to in different circumstances. That tape was copied not by the OTP but by the Audio-Visual Unit straightaway, and copies of that tape, master copies, were distributed to everyone. The Defence and, indeed, the witness himself wanted to take a copy home with him, and I think he had one. That second tape was then presented in due course to the Evidence Unit in the same way as the earlier one had been presented much earlier. Now, at that moment and from that moment on, master copies were the exhibit, effectively, and the possession of the original tapes remained with the OTP and were well known to remain with the OTP, for the Chamber will recall that the next issue about the tapes was whether tape 1, the first tape, was identical in content to tape 2. And Mr. Stein, who then appeared for the defendant, came to our office or to an office here in order that he could listen to and compare both tapes, one with the other. So it's always been known by the Defence that we had possession of those tapes. Following that exercise, the tapes, both of them, were returned to the Evidence Unit. Nothing had been made clear in cross-examination as to what was being said about the tape or as to which bits of it were not accurate or otherwise. There was no material cross-examination at all. I think, and I'll be corrected by Ms. Verhaag, if I'm wrong, about the order of events, but I think the next thing that happened was we got a summary of the Defence witnesses, but I'm not sure whether it was that way around or not. But, in any event, when we got a summary of the Defence witnesses, again absolute imprecision, save to say that some expert was identified as going to speak about the tape no doubt on the basis of the master copy in the possession of the Defence. We have no reason to believe in this case that we are going to get more than the minimum three weeks' notice for experts' reports, or whatever it may be, and so at that stage it was decided, it not having been thought necessary earlier, to see what, if anything, an expert could say of this tape so as, at least to that extent, to be ready to deal, in the short period of time, with whatever the Defence expert may say. The experts identified were those who have been used by the Tribunal or for the Tribunal before here in Holland. They asked to see the original original, as it were, and it was signed out under chain of custody to them, digitally copied, and has, in due course, been returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is that document, the original original, which should be in the custody of the Registry. People should have copies, including the Prosecution and the Defence. But what is wrong is that the Prosecution has the original, and it's that item -- I called it a document -- that item that should be in the custody of the Registry, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I may say so, in that case I accept that if we, between us, articulated the position more, that's almost certainly what would have happened and that particular exhibit would have been under -- either gone to the Registry or -- and this is an alternative that I mention without discussing it too much with Ms. Greenwood, save in the most general terms -- or in respect of such exhibits, that they be marked not to be moved from the secure environment in which they, we say, exist, save on notice. And I make that last point, I think, for this reason: I'm just going to check something first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, there's nothing else I want to add following on my last observation. But there is this: Exhibits that are in the Evidence Unit of this type are under a strict chain of custody recording system. I'm not going to go into the detail for obvious reasons, because it's a secure system, and I can -- possibly in other circumstances, the Chamber would like to know, and probably at some stage and in some setting, that wouldn't be a bad idea. But it's an extremely strict system, because as you may have been able to glance through the document, all exhibits have, as their underlying purpose, not only the instant trial but other investigations in the continuing functioning of this place, another reason for keeping them perhaps in one place and in atmospherically-good conditions, so far as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You don't object to the Defence keeping exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, on the same basis that if we ask to see an original, no doubt the best original will be produced to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And you invite us to ignore the Rule, as has been done?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, I don't invite you to ignore the Rule. Two points on that. There's Rule 41, which I've already drawn to your attention, which is the duty to us to keep exhibits for investigations which are continuing. But I respectfully suggest that the proper approach in these documentary cases can be to say that the exhibit is -- the master copy of the document is the exhibit. But, of course, at any stage up until deliberations, probably any stage up until appeal, any party can require the original original to be produced for consideration, and that could always be done. I think conceptually that is the proper way to look at it, and then there is no breach of the Rules because what is produced, which is what has been produced here, is a master copy. And in the same way as some of our original originals are copies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may interrupt you just for a second, Mr. Nice. Why is it said that exhibits need to be kept carefully by a neutral authority because they serve as -- you say Judge May and Judge Robinson have to decide on the innocence or guilt of somebody, that is, [indiscernible]. Why is it said that exhibits -- we're not inventing anything new, that they need to be kept without the reach of parties concerned so that there can be no alteration possible. That is the problem, so that one really is assured that no alterations, no changes, are made. You say that this is an exception, that something really exceptional is needed to have something changed, because an exhibit is such and such, and this alteration, if it is done, then it has to be evidently well done, and so on and so forth. But there is a practical matter in this regard, and that is to avoid, indeed, all the alterations of any exhibit. You are saying that we are now involved in a case based on documents. In a documentary case, does that change anything? You know well that here there are texts which are barely legible, one cannot see very well, and I suppose they will be less legible as time goes by. Here we have only text. It is the fact that there is nothing else but the text, most of the exhibits are text. Now, you're saying we are following a particular practice in the Tribunal, in our Tribunal, that the things were organised in such and such a manner. My idea is that we shall have to decide about the audiotape which has stirred all this, the audiotape. As for the problem in general, I believe that will have to be raised at the institutional level, as you said. We shall do it. Don't worry about that where the institutions are -- and I think this matter will have to be discussed in depth, so that we shall raise this matter. As for the specific case, the audiotape, if there is a master copy, it should be kept with the Registry and you should have a copy of it, and that is all. I believe that is the principal that I shall have to raise, of course, with my colleagues and speaking in my own name, and we shall have to discuss it at the institutional level and we shall have to then -- because this is an institutional problem, it will have to be discussed at the institutional level. That is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I need only make two points in answer to that. Obviously --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I need only make two points in answer to that. First, there is, of course, no reason to have any distrust of the OTP, historically or otherwise, and the suggestion that any document would ever be altered is, of course, one that is -- it's hard to say "resisted" and I don't want to say "offensive", but it's obviously one that we don't in any sense accept. But since Your Honour raises it, the answer is rather reassuring and it's why, under a modern system, what we're doing is actually entirely appropriate. When the document comes in, it is electronically scanned. The number goes on it, and that freezes for all time the appearance of the document at that stage. Whether it degrades, which happens with, of course, fax paper and which is one of the great advantages of scanning material as soon as it comes in -- so it's scanned, it has a unique number. The numbers can indeed tell you something, obviously, about when the document arrives. It's all quite useful material. So alteration of the document isn't a possibility, and it is that exact reflection of the original that is distributed to all parties, either in advance of the trial or at the trial, and that system of security -- and I make no complaint about this -- is bound to be far greater than we can expect, we prosecutors can expect, using the plural to reflect other Chambers, from the Defence, who of course will have an original original of whatever they produce in copy form to the Court but who necessarily won't have the regimes of processing that a big institution like this does have, so that in many ways, as I have been attempting to explain, what you have here is a much more secure system, and its security is more likely to be compromised by moving it from -- moving the paper exhibits routinely from one well-ordered and comprehensive system to various different trolleys around the place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think we've heard all this, with great respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: With respect, we've heard this. You have still not dealt with the perception of the International Community, but we'll leave that aside. Now, we've heard the submissions. We're not in a position to make a ruling, and it's now 10 to 4.00. But I would like to hear Mr. Sayers on the matter, unless there's something you particularly want to raise, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. You take me to task over not dealing with the perception of the International Community. I deal with that by identifying the secure systems and, in particular -- and I repeat this -- by saying that on either side, when an original is wanted, it's available, and that that, in our submission, is a proper way of dealing with this and with this type of case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, one point we have to consider in all this is whether there has, in fact, been any prejudice beyond the notion of perception as a result of what we have discovered about the way the exhibits have been kept. Now, we've identified the audiotape as a particular sensitive and crucial piece of evidence which the authenticity of which, I understand, that you're challenging. Now, is there any other exhibit that you say should be the subject of an immediate order if we may have to consider this as it's being suggested institutionally, and that is looking at other cases too, but clearly the audiotape is in a different category from anything else. I can say that I, myself, cannot think of any, but there may be some which you would consider. It may be that you would like to think about it over night.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, I can give you a reaction, Mr. President, right now, if you wish, and I'm more than happy to elaborate on it tomorrow. To answer your particular question, there are over 2300 exhibits in this case. It's not fair, I think, to ask us to remember off the cuff as it were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's why I said think about it and until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I was just going to use as one example the document that was produced yesterday. How in the world could anybody have any faith in that kind of a document? I don't have the exhibit number to mind but I'm sure the Court knows exactly what I'm talking about. A document that supposedly commemorates the anniversary of Sveti Duh company, a company that existed unrebutted and unreputed testimony of the witness for about three months and was founded in February 27th, 1992, yet this document was dated August sometime, I believe, and had another document attached to it of as said yesterday, indeterminate parentage with someone's scratchings on the front of it. Who knows where those documents come from? And I would absolutely like to see the originals of documents such as that. That's what we've been trying to do throughout ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, Mr. Sayers, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: ... making our foundation objections. Surely, it shouldn't be up to the Defence, once these documents flow in tidal waves into the record, to show that they are not authentic. It's the burden of the Prosecution to show that they are authentic, and that's just by way of one problem. But let me just step back a little if I may and address the question that seems to be before the Court today. There are really two issues. The question of exhibits generally, obviously, and I'll have to take a look at the Prosecution's submission on that. But what brought us here wasn't exhibits generally, and no amount of sophistry, no amount of fog, no amount of argument can simply confuse or conceal the fact that there's been a serious wrong committed here. Let me just go back to the exhibit at issue, the tape, it's Exhibit 2801.4, and I'd like to read this into the record, page 13747 where Mr. Nice said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the court will recall that Mr. Husic produced the original videotape in the court. That's the tape we're talking about, not any other tape, that tape. And here's what Mr. Nice said, "In those circumstances may the witness please produce the tape, hand it to the usher. Can it be marked as Exhibit 2801.4. It better be marked I suppose 2801.4," and that's exactly what happened. And under those circumstances Rule 81 comes into play. And I might say that the considerations of justice that was articulated by one member of the bench are absolutely the foundation of what we're dealing with here: Justice. Justice and the administration of justice; fairness and equality. The very principles are enshrined in Article 21 and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence breathe substance and life into those principles. And Rule 81(C), I would submit to the Court, couldn't be clearer, "The Registrar shall retain and preserve all physical evidence of it during the proceedings subject to any practice direction..." and I don't believe there is one, and certainly one hasn't been pointed to by the Prosecution, "... or any ordinary which a Chamber may make at any time with respect to control or disposition, the physical evidence of it during proceedings before that Chamber." Now we find notwithstanding the plethora of copies of this alleged unitary tape floating around in the -- in our files in the Prosecution's files and in the Court's files. Well, I don't even know -- well, I do not know even know whether they are in the Court's files. But this document, of all documents, is one that should be in the Registry and we find, and found out for the first time last week, that it never was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, I suspect you are pushing at an open door on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where this tape should be, the original of this tape, not any sort of copy, even if it can be called a master copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, I think copies and master copies, Your Honour, that's just the fog of confusion. We're talking about an exhibit, an exhibit in this trial which should be in the Registry and is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us now consider the position. Are you first of all asking us to make any order in respect of the original of the two audio tapes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, I think that the tapes should be stricken from evidence. Well, it's not in evidence. I don't know how you can strike it from evidence, but it should not be received into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is in evidence. It's been exhibited. It's a question of where the original should be. We will deal with that application in due course. If you -- it may be a matter which we should call for a response in writing from the Prosecution to your application on that. Meanwhile, on a practical level, have you got the original as we ordered last week?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We have not got the original. We have a digital audiotape copy of it. As the Judge -- as Your Honour points out, I think that that is what was ordered and that's been complied with and we've received that from the Registry. I want to make it perfectly clear, I have no criticism of the Registry throughout this. We have had nothing but the most professional relations with the Registry. They have conducted themselves in a perfectly practical and audible way. Nonetheless, it has to be shocking to any attorney in a criminal case, to find out that an exhibit, especially an exhibit like this has gone AWOL. I've never heard of such a situation in any case in any court even the lowliest court in a national jurisdiction. And yet -- well, I think I've said all -- I cannot believe that the Prosecution tries to defend this situation and argue that it, in fact, has not done -- well, I've made my point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think we have it. Rhetoric aside, let us consider the position. What are you -- we will deal with the audiotape and make what order we think appropriate in relation to that. We have to consider what should be done about the other exhibits and, of course, that would include Defence exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you -- do you want to make any submissions about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, in the matter of exhibits generally, it seems that where the accuracy of the copy is not contested as it has not been for the majority of these exhibits, I believe, that in this institution, as well as in most national jurisdictions, copies are as admissible as the originals providing there's no challenge to the authenticity of the originals. But where there is a challenge to the authenticity, then it seems to me a basic proposition of fair and equality and justice that that original should be produced so that the Court can be satisfied, itself, that it actually -- that the original document exists and it's not some sort of a fake as that document appeared to be yesterday or there are other problems with it. But that seems the regimen that we've been following where there is contest of the accuracy of the copy, there cannot be objection to the admission into evidence of that copy. But where there is a challenge to the authenticity of that document, then clearly the original should be produced and it should be the only place that is permitted by the Rules and in the Court, with the Registry of the Court, and not within a party especially in a criminal case. I think that's a fair statement of our position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with the leave, on behalf of Mr. Cerkez's Defence, I should like to articulate our position. And it, of course, fully tallies with the position of the Defence of Mr. Kordic. What I should like to add to all of this is that the Defence considers Rule 81(C) completely clear and our interpretation is that the moment an exhibit has been produced and admitted, and gets its number from the Registry, then it must be the Registry along with Rule 81(C) which will take care of that particular exhibit. I do not think that that rule can be changed, amended, as long as that it is in force and, in particular, but unilateral decision of one party to the proceedings. We are not disputing that the secure system that my learned friend from the Prosecution spoke about is good. Our question is who controls that secure system? I simply see no reason why the same system of the safe-keeping of exhibits could not be under the Registry control as Rule 81(C) makes it possible. So that is the position of Mr. Cerkez's Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In relation to the audiotape, the number of which was given by Mr. Nice 2810.4, I think, that is to be forthwith, the original is to be forthwith handed into the custody of the Registry. In relation to Mr. Sayers' application that it be excluded from evidence, we will entertain that application and rule upon it in due course. In order to do so, and before we rule on it, we would wish to have from the Prosecution a written document setting out where the tape has been since it was produced in Court by the witness and then, in due course, if we could have that within seven days, we will consider what steps, if any, are needed to take the matter forward. In relation to the other exhibits, we shall consider the situation and decide what should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I suggest that you make the order not only in respect of the second tape that was produced by the witness but that if you're going to make that order, but you also make it in respect of the first tape which, as you will recall, was listened to and was found to be identical to the second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, both tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Both tapes. And that will be done forthwith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Tomorrow morning, and we will consider the affidavits half past nine.
